K-Modes

2024-07-11

K-modes is a clustering algorithm designed specifically to handle categorical data. K-modes replaces the cluster mean used in K-means with the mode—the most frequent value for each categorical variable. It calculates the distance between data points using a matching dissimilarity measure that counts the number of mismatches between categorical variables. K-modes can be more effective than K-means when working with categorical data.

In summary, K-means is a clustering algorithm that works well with numerical data, whereas K-modes is a clustering algorithm designed specifically to handle categorical data.

Load database

You need to have run at least the initial part of the LCA—not the entire LCA, but enough to establish the baseline used for all the analyses. I’m taking the comorbidities from that.

myMMcondition[,2:ncol(myMMcondition)] = apply(myMMcondition[,2:ncol(myMMcondition)], 2, function(x) as.numeric(as.character(x)));
nrow(myMMcondition)

The rest: show results

Cargo resultados

By default, simple matching distance is used to determine the dissimilarity between two objects. It is calculated by counting the number of dissimilarities across all variables. Alternatively, this distance can be weighted based on category frequencies in the data (see Huang, 1997, for details).

Methods: https://uc-r.github.io/kmeans_clustering#silo

Elbow method

The goal is to define clusters such that the total within-cluster variation (total within-cluster sum of squares) is minimized. The location of the “elbow” or bend in the TWSS plot is typically considered an indicator of the appropriate number of clusters.

withindiff: simple matching distances within the group for each cluster. This represents SW—the standard deviation of a specific group.

The sum of SW values—that is, SSW (sum of squares within clusters; note that this differs from TWSS, where SSB = TSS - SSW)—can be calculated by summing these figures across all groups. As the number of clusters increases, SSW is expected to decrease. This SSW value itself can serve as a metric for cluster validation.

https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1757-899X/1087/1/012085/pdf

num_clusters <- 1:length(myresult)
SSW <- c()
for (k in num_clusters) {
  SSW <- c(SSW, sum(myresult[[k]][["withindiff"]])) # cogido de internet
                                                    # literal, o sea bien
}
par(bg = '#E0FFFF') # background

     col = "#B4CDCD", # Grid line color
     lwd = 1))
lines(num_clusters, SSW, lwd =1, col='#4169E1')

axis(1, at = seq(1, 7, by = 1)) # eje y 

axis(2, at = seq(76000, 125000, by = 6800)) # eje y

par(mfrow = c(1,1))

SSW is the sum of squared differences between a value and its sample mean across all values. The model attempts to minimize this measure of model quality. This is known as the Within-Cluster Sum of Squares (WCSS), which is the sum of the distances between data points and their corresponding centroid for each cluster. The lower this quality measure, the closer we get to the optimal model (a process performed by the algorithm).

Looking at the graphs and the maximum values ​​(the other clusters in each group are smaller, of course)… the more we increase the number of groups, the smaller the metric becomes (which is to be expected). Fewer than 3 clusters makes no clinical sense. With 3 clusters, the metric seems too high… From 4 clusters onwards, the metric drops significantly; 4 is a good choice. I would lean towards 5 clusters: firstly, because the largest cluster value drops by more than 2,000 compared to the largest one with 4 clusters; and secondly, because it appears to yield 4 similar groups plus just one “catch-all” group—which makes sense, as it avoids having a mix of very good groups and very odd ones. With this algorithm, I would also consider other metrics or examine the clinical significance of the clusters themselves.

This cannot be done with categorical or factor data; it will cause an error later. Set the data to numeric.

Set any k you want

This next function calculates the average silhouette width, just like “fviz_nbclust”, but I trust the latter more than others

# function to compute average silhouette for k clusters

avg_sil <- function(k) {
  km.res <- myresult[[k]][["cluster"]]
  ss <- cluster::silhouette(x=km.res, dist=distancias)
  # calcular el ancho de silueta promedio
  mean(ss[, 3])
}

# Compute and plot wss
k.values <- 2:7 # no sale con 1
# extract avg silhouette
avg_sil_values <- purrr::map_dbl(k.values, avg_sil)
par(bg = '#E0FFFF') # background


plot(k.values, avg_sil_values, axes = FALSE,   # va del 0.05 al 0.12 aprox
       type = "b", pch = 19, frame = FALSE, 
       xlab = "Number of clusters",
       ylab = "Average Silhouettes",
     col='#4169E1', ylim = c(0.0, 0.20), panel.first=grid(lty = 1,      # Grid line type
                                                                                                                                                                                        col = "#B4CDCD", # Grid line color
                                                                                                                                                                                        lwd = 1))

lines(k.values, avg_sil_values, lwd =1, col='#4169E1')

abline(v = which.max(avg_sil_values)+1, col = c("#27408B"),
       lwd = 1,
       lty = 2:3)
    # +1 porque el 1 es en realidad 2 clusters

axis(1, k.values) # eje y 

axis(2, at = seq(0, 0.2, by = 0.04), las=2)

The silhouette value is a measure of how similar an object is to its own cluster (cohesion) compared to other clusters (separation). The silhouette ranges from −1 to +1, where a high value indicates that the object is well-matched to its own cluster and poorly matched to neighboring clusters. In short, the average silhouette method measures the quality of a clustering—that is, it determines how well each object is positioned within its cluster. A high average silhouette width indicates good clustering. The average silhouette method calculates the average silhouette of the observations for different values ​​of k. The optimal number of clusters, k, is the one that maximizes the average silhouette across a range of possible values ​​for k.

It appears that 7, 2, and 4 clusters maximize the average silhouette values, in that order. The result for 3 is not good… However, according to the following—which is a summary of this—the best option is 3, followed by 4, then 6. Theoretically, it is better to rely on the final result. And also on the 3-cluster option.

I place more trust in this (IT IS THE SAME THING; both represent the mean average silhouette width):
